title: 1 Chronicles 17:1–15
context: 1 Chronicles 17 parallels 2 Samuel 7, where the Davidic covenant is discussed more fully; the notes here point to that treatment rather than repeat it. David proposes to build a house for the ark, Nathan first approves, and God answers that David will not build him a house; instead the LORD will build David a house. God promises to raise up David’s offspring, establish his throne forever, be his father, and not withdraw his loving kindness. Chronicles differs from Samuel in several details, including the absence of the clause about chastening iniquity (2 Samuel 7:14) and the phrase “my house and in my kingdom” (17:14). Both traditions read the promise as shared ground: the line secure by God’s oath, individual kings accountable, and the promise fulfilled in Christ.

verses.text: When David was living in his house, David said to Nathan the prophet, “Behold, I live in a cedar house, but the ark of the LORD’s covenant is in a tent.”
verses.arminianNotes:
Living in his house, David tells Nathan that he lives in a cedar house while the ark of the covenant is in a tent. The parallel is 2 Samuel 7:1–2.

Arminian readers see David’s desire to honor God freely arising in a time of settled blessing.
verses.reformedNotes:
Chronicles does not include 2 Samuel 7:1’s note that the LORD had given David rest from his enemies; the reason for the omission is not stated.

Reformed readers see the scene framed for God’s initiative. Both traditions read this as shared ground.

verses.text: Nathan said to David, “Do all that is in your heart; for God is with you.”
verses.arminianNotes:
Nathan tells David to do all that is in his heart, for God is with him. The prophet’s first response is encouraging.

Arminian readers see a reasonable human judgment, offered in good faith before God speaks.
verses.reformedNotes:
Where 2 Samuel 7:3 says the LORD is with David, Chronicles here reads God, one of several small wording differences.

Reformed readers see that even a true prophet’s counsel waits on God’s word. Both traditions read this as shared ground, as in the 2 Samuel 7 notes.

verses.text: That same night, the word of God came to Nathan, saying,
verses.arminianNotes:
That same night, the word of God comes to Nathan. God answers quickly.

Arminian readers see God personally engaging with David’s proposal and responding to it, as the parallel account in 2 Samuel 7:4 also shows.
verses.reformedNotes:
The timing stresses that the plan is not settled by human enthusiasm. God himself redirects it.

Reformed readers see the LORD’s sovereign initiative in the covenant that follows. Both traditions read this plainly as shared ground about the priority of God’s word.

verses.text: “Go and tell David my servant, ‘The LORD says, “You shall not build me a house to dwell in;
verses.arminianNotes:
God tells Nathan to say to David, his servant, that he will not build God a house to dwell in. The answer is a firm no.

Arminian readers see God gently but clearly redirecting a sincere desire.
verses.reformedNotes:
In 2 Samuel 7:5 the refusal is framed as a question; Chronicles states it directly. The Chronicler does not explain the difference.

Reformed readers see God reserving the building for his chosen time and person. Both traditions read this as shared ground.

verses.text: for I have not lived in a house since the day that I brought up Israel to this day, but have gone from tent to tent, and from one tent to another.
verses.arminianNotes:
God says he has not lived in a house since bringing up Israel, but has gone from tent to tent. His presence has moved with his people.

Arminian readers see God’s willingness to dwell among his people as they journey.
verses.reformedNotes:
The wording differs slightly from 2 Samuel 7:6, but the point is the same: God has not asked for a fixed house.

Reformed readers see God’s freedom and condescension in dwelling with Israel. Both traditions read this plainly as shared ground.

verses.text: In all places in which I have walked with all Israel, did I speak a word with any of the judges of Israel, whom I commanded to be shepherd of my people, saying, ‘Why have you not built me a house of cedar?’ ” ’
verses.arminianNotes:
God asks whether he ever told any of Israel’s judges, whom he appointed to shepherd his people, to build him a house of cedar. He never did.

Arminian readers see that David’s plan, though sincere, was not commanded.
verses.reformedNotes:
Chronicles reads judges where 2 Samuel 7:7 reads tribes of Israel. The narrative leaves the difference unexplained.

Reformed readers see God setting the terms of his worship. Both traditions read this as shared ground about God’s initiative in his own house.

verses.text: “Now therefore, you shall tell my servant David, ‘The LORD of Armies says, “I took you from the sheep pen, from following the sheep, to be prince over my people Israel.
verses.arminianNotes:
The LORD of Armies recalls taking David from following the sheep to be prince over Israel. David’s rise is God’s doing.

Arminian readers see grace calling a shepherd to a task he did not seek.
verses.reformedNotes:
The shepherd image ties David’s past to his calling as shepherd of God’s people, as in 2 Samuel 7:8.

Reformed readers see God’s free choice of David. Both traditions read this as shared ground about grace preceding David’s service and grounding the promise that follows.

verses.text: I have been with you wherever you have gone, and have cut off all your enemies from before you. I will make you a name like the name of the great ones who are on the earth.
verses.arminianNotes:
God has been with David wherever he went, cut off his enemies, and will make him a name like the great ones of the earth. Past faithfulness grounds future promise.

Arminian readers see God’s steady presence through David’s life.
verses.reformedNotes:
The promise of a great name may recall the promise to Abraham of a great name (Genesis 12:2).

Reformed readers see God building David’s name for his own purposes. Both traditions read this as shared ground and, as in 2 Samuel 7:9, see the promise fulfilled.

verses.text: I will appoint a place for my people Israel, and will plant them, that they may dwell in their own place, and be moved no more. The children of wickedness will not waste them any more, as at the first,
verses.arminianNotes:
God will appoint a place for Israel, plant them, and they will no longer be troubled by the children of wickedness as at first. The promise extends to the people.

Arminian readers see God’s care for Israel as a whole, not only its king.
verses.reformedNotes:
The planting image speaks of security and permanence. The covenant with David serves the good of Israel.

Reformed readers see God’s purpose for his people carried by the king’s line. Both traditions read this as shared ground, consistent with 2 Samuel 7:10.

verses.text: and from the day that I commanded judges to be over my people Israel. I will subdue all your enemies. Moreover I tell you that the LORD will build you a house.
verses.arminianNotes:
God will subdue David’s enemies and declares that the LORD will build David a house. The wordplay turns from temple to dynasty.

Arminian readers see God’s generosity far exceeding David’s offer.
verses.reformedNotes:
Where 2 Samuel 7:11 promises rest from enemies, Chronicles speaks of subduing them, and its parallel says the LORD will make David a house.

Reformed readers see the covenant as God’s gift, not David’s achievement. Both traditions read this as clear shared ground.

verses.text: It will happen, when your days are fulfilled that you must go to be with your fathers, that I will set up your offspring after you, who will be of your sons; and I will establish his kingdom.
verses.arminianNotes:
When David’s days are fulfilled, God will raise up his offspring, one of his sons, and establish his kingdom. The promise reaches past David’s death.

Arminian readers see the promise first fulfilled in Solomon and finally in Christ, as the 2 Samuel 7 notes say.
verses.reformedNotes:
Chronicles reads “who will be of your sons” where 2 Samuel 7:12 reads “who will proceed out of your body.” The sense is close.

Reformed readers see the line of promise reaching to Christ. Both traditions read this as shared ground.

verses.text: He will build me a house, and I will establish his throne forever.
verses.arminianNotes:
The offspring will build God a house, and God will establish his throne forever. Temple and throne are joined.

Arminian readers see Solomon’s temple as a first fulfillment, with the eternal throne pointing beyond him to Christ.
verses.reformedNotes:
2 Samuel 7:13 speaks of a house for God’s name; Chronicles simply says a house for God.

Reformed readers see the eternal throne fulfilled in Christ. Both traditions read this as messianic common ground, consistent with the 2 Samuel 7 notes, and need not restate that discussion here.

verses.text: I will be his father, and he will be my son. I will not take my loving kindness away from him, as I took it from him who was before you;
verses.arminianNotes:
God will be his father, and he will be God’s son, and God will not take away his loving kindness as he did from the one before David. The promise is steadfast.

Arminian readers see God binding himself to David’s line in grace.
verses.reformedNotes:
Chronicles lacks the clause in 2 Samuel 7:14 about chastening the son if he commits iniquity, and refers to Saul only as “him who was before you.”

Reformed readers see covenant love that will not be withdrawn. Both traditions read this as shared ground.

verses.text: but I will settle him in my house and in my kingdom forever. His throne will be established forever.” ’ ”
verses.arminianNotes:
God will settle the son in “my house and in my kingdom forever,” and his throne will be established forever. The wording centers on God’s own house and kingdom.

Arminian readers see the Davidic king serving within God’s reign.
verses.reformedNotes:
2 Samuel 7:16 reads “Your house and your kingdom.” Many readers suggest Chronicles stresses that the kingdom is ultimately God’s, though the text does not explain the change.

Reformed readers see the throne secured by God himself. Both traditions read this as shared ground fulfilled in Christ.

verses.text: According to all these words, and according to all this vision, so Nathan spoke to David.
verses.arminianNotes:
Nathan speaks to David according to all these words and all this vision. The prophet delivers the message faithfully.

Arminian readers see Nathan setting aside his earlier counsel to speak exactly what God gave him.
verses.reformedNotes:
The closing note matches 2 Samuel 7:17 and calls the message a vision.

Reformed readers see the prophet’s faithfulness to God’s word over his own first opinion. Both traditions read this plainly as shared ground about faithful prophetic speech and the reliability of the promise David has received.
